item.research_question: How can nanoscale multi-principal element intermetallic (MPEI) nanoparticles with up to eight elements be synthesized without particle growth, agglomeration, or phase separation, which are common issues in traditional annealing methods?
item.material_system: Octonary (Pt0.8Pd0.1Au0.1)(Fe0.6Co0.1Ni0.1Cu0.1Sn0.1), quinary Pt(Fe0.7Co0.1Ni0.1Cu0.1), and binary PtFe intermetallic nanoparticles; disordered solid-solution high-entropy alloy (HEA) precursors
item.processing_route: Joule heating of metal salt precursors on a carbonized wood substrate: initial rapid thermal shock for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K to form HEA nanoparticles, followed by reheating at ~1100 K for ~5 min to induce disorder-to-order transition, and rapid cooling at ~10^4 K/s to lock the structure
item.test_conditions: XRD characterization at ~1100 K; in situ STEM heating at ~1100 K for up to 60 min; Monte Carlo simulations at 1100 K; high-temperature oxide melt drop solution calorimetry at 700°C; electrochemical testing in 1 M KOH + 1 M ethanol at 0.2 to 1.2 V vs RHE
key_findings: Ultrasmall MPEI nanoparticles with sizes of 4 to 5 nm were synthesized containing up to eight elements (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) without phase separation.
The long-range ordering (LRO) parameter increased from 10% (0.5 s heating) to ~100% (5 min heating) at ~1100 K, confirming the disorder-to-order transition.
Particles larger than ~60 nm failed to achieve full ordering (LRO < 40% in simulations for 10.8 nm particles) and exhibited phase separation or disordered structures.
Calorimetry showed the enthalpy change from quinary HEA to MPEI was -0.20 eV per formula unit, and for octonary HEA to MPEI was -0.32 eV per formula unit, indicating thermodynamic favorability.
Octonary MPEI nanoparticles demonstrated ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR) activity 8 times higher than binary PtFe intermetallic and 12 times higher than commercial Pt/C catalyst.
MPEI nanoparticles maintained a fully ordered L10 structure after 60 min of additional heating at ~1100 K, whereas binary PtFe nanoparticles transformed to a disordered alloy after 60 min.
Traditional annealing (~1100 K for 3 hours) of the octonary composition resulted in phase-separated heterostructures with large particle sizes (~76.2 ± 4.2 nm).
The L10 intermetallic structure features two sublattices where noble metals (Pt, Pd, Au) occupy one sublattice and non-noble metals (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Sn) occupy the other.
item.mechanism: The disorder-to-order transition is driven by the lower surface energy of MPEIs compared to HEAs, which is significant in ultrasmall nanoparticles due to their large relative surface area; the transition is thermodynamically favored (ΔG < 0) at synthesis temperatures (~1100 K) due to strong atom-atom interactions (spin-orbit coupling and hybridization) that lower the formation enthalpy, while rapid cooling kinetically traps the ordered structure and prevents growth.
item.limitations: The disorder-to-order transition to a fully ordered single-phase MPEI cannot be achieved for particles larger than ~5 nm (e.g., 10 to 20 nm or 150 nm) due to higher energy barriers and decreased surface energy effects; traditional annealing methods inherently cause phase separation and particle growth in multimetallic systems.
item.future_work: The findings can be extended to produce a combinatorial library of intermetallic nanomaterials with novel properties and applications, potentially inducing a new frontier of intermetallic research in catalysis, magnetics, and superconductivity.
quotes: We apply just 5 min of Joule heating to promote the phase transition of the nanoparticles into L10 intermetallic structure, which is then preserved by rapidly cooling.
MPEI nanoparticles demonstrate improved EOR activity that is 8 and 12 times higher than the binary PtFe intermetallic and commercial Pt/C catalyst, respectively.
